story.title: A Wave of Molasses Killed 21 People in Boston
story.topic: The Great Molasses Flood, Boston North End, 15 January 1919: a leaking, brown-painted molasses tank burst; 21 dead; owners found liable; engineering sign-off rules followed
story.angle: It sounds like a joke, but syrup killed 21 people: physics (dense, thickening in the cold) plus a leak the company painted over
story.centralQuestion: How does a tank of syrup kill twenty-one people?
story.coreEmotion: disbelief turning to grim respect, ending wry
story.takeaway: Weight, cold, and ignored warnings killed 21 people; that is partly why engineers must still sign for their math
story.tone: wry hook, grave middle, dry ending
story.sensitivity: Real tragedy: no bodies, no struggling victims, no jokes about the dead; humour only in the premise and the idiom; company figures are generic, no named individual blamed on screen

weaknesses.issue: Needs a molasses-wave card and flood sheet (F01), a North End set with the tank (F02) and explainer props (F03); the wave is the hook and cannot be faked cheaply. Scored 7: 3 sets (1 adapted, the street adapts the built bombay-1944 city + kit dock.ts), minus 1 for the unbuilt wave card.
'Taller than a bus' rests on the 15 ft estimate (Mass Moments, History.com); one source gives 8-15 ft. Kept as a comparison, range in the description.
'Many victims died because they were stuck' softens Rubinstein's single-expert 'about half' (CSMonitor); 1.5x density has one source read (History.com).

129 words: rhythm.py estimates 52.1 s (marked) / 49.6 s (clean) vs the 47 s target (+5-11%). At Brian +10% (~2.77 w/s measured on Tunguska) real audio should land ~49-51 s; retime from words.json. If it runs long, cut 'They still do.' or 'they say'.
The open question is answered at ~65-69% (31.8-35.8 s of 52 s), slightly before the requested ~70%.
At 47 s there is no room for a named victim; the human cost is carried by 'twenty-one people' and the rescuer shot only.
'Tell us below' was cut; the comment ask is the question alone (no CTA wording). The idiom 'slow as molasses' may be unfamiliar to some non-US viewers; the hook image carries the loop anyway.

publishing.description:
On 15 January 1919, a storage tank holding about 2.3 million gallons of molasses burst in Boston's North End. The wave, estimated at around 35 mph and somewhere between 15 and 25 feet high (estimates range from 8 to 40 ft), killed 21 people and injured about 150. Molasses is far denser than water, and as it cooled in the January air it thickened, trapping victims and slowing rescuers. Neighbours said the tank had leaked since it was filled in 1915; instead of fixing it, the company had it painted brown. A court-appointed auditor later found the owner, United States Industrial Alcohol, liable, and Boston began requiring engineers' calculations to be filed and plans signed and stamped.
Sources: Mass Moments (https://www.massmoments.org/moment-details.html?mid=19); City of Boston (https://www.boston.gov/ar/news/100-years-ago-today-molasses-crashes-through-bostons-north-end); HISTORY.com, the science of the flood (https://www.history.com/articles/great-molasses-flood-science); AP/Boston.com on the 2016 Harvard fluid-dynamics study (https://www.boston.com/news/history/2016/11/24/slow-as-molasses-sweet-but-deadly-1919-disaster-explained); Christian Science Monitor (https://www.csmonitor.com/layout/set/amphtml/Science/2016/1129/Scientists-finally-decode-the-Great-Molasses-Flood-of-1919); NBC News / Stephen Puleo, Dark Tide (https://www.euronews.com/2019/01/15/great-boston-molasses-flood-1919-killed-21-after-2-million-n958326); The Straight Dope (https://www.straightdope.com/21343697/was-boston-once-literally-flooded-with-molasses); Wikipedia, Great Molasses Flood (for its cited sources).
publishing.pinnedComment: Numbers note: nobody measured the wave. Height estimates run from about 8 to 40 feet (15 and 25 ft are the most quoted), speed around 35 mph. One Harvard researcher estimated about half the victims died because they were stuck. And the folklore: for decades, locals said the North End smelled of molasses on hot days. Would you have lived next to that tank?
